title: Connection and Conversation
reflection: Where could I open a door this week, perhaps side by side while doing something together, so that my child feels fully heard?

questions.q: According to Lesson 11, what does a child’s growing silence at home tell a parent?
o: The child has outgrown the family and now looks to friends for what he needs.
The child is hiding something, and the parent should find out what it is.
The channel has grown less healthy and needs some care; it is no one’s failing.
The child’s friends online offer more than the parent ever could.
questions.e: That silence is a message. Children are hungry for attention, and long for someone to acknowledge that they can think for themselves. If they do not find this with their parents, they look elsewhere and little by little withdraw. Most quiet spells are normal, but if withdrawal lasts for weeks or comes with changes in sleep, eating or mood, speak to a doctor or counsellor.
questions.c: Silence is a message that the channel needs care

questions.q: A mother answered “Lovely, darling” without looking up when her twelve-year-old showed her a model plane he had spent two hours building. Which step fits Lesson 11?
o: Explain that she was busy that evening, so that he understands why she did not look.
Praise the plane warmly in front of the family, to make up for the missed moment.
Ask him outright why he has stopped telling her things, and listen to his answer.
Find the plane that evening, and ask him how he made the wings.
questions.e: A moment can be met differently tomorrow. The best conversations rarely happen face to face but side by side. Draw out his ideas, encourage his thinking, and give back the heart of what he says: “Did I get you right?” That tells him he has been heard, and a child who feels heard comes to know that he belongs.
questions.c: Being truly heard: the door to the parent’s mind and heart stands open

questions.q: “A parent’s calm or worry reaches a child only through what the parent says.”
questions.e: Between a parent and a child far more is said than is ever spoken. A parent who is calm, balanced and poised passes that on without a word, and anxiety, anger and worry pass across in the same silent way. The child takes in whatever we carry.
questions.c: Far more is said between parent and child than is ever spoken

questions.q: A parent who has only a few spare minutes each day wonders whether it is worth trying to connect. Which view fits Lesson 11?
o: Wait for a weekend, when there are hours to give, and do it properly then.
A few minutes of whole attention give what hours of half-attention never will.
Keep the child close all evening while doing other things, so as not to miss anything.
Make up for the lack of time with small gifts that show the parent cares.
questions.e: How deeply anything reaches a child depends on attention. When a parent turns the whole mind toward the child, communication is swift and sure, and much can pass in a very short time. When attention is scattered, half on the child and half elsewhere, the channel struggles to open at all.
questions.c: A few minutes of whole attention give what hours of half-attention never will

questions.q: According to Lesson 11, why does the lesson ask a parent to speak what is true and endearing?
o: Because children cannot bear hard truths, and pleasant words are simply easier to hear.
Because what passes between hearts is the speaker’s intent and energy, which words carry.
Because kind words persuade a child more quickly than blunt ones.
Because a parent who speaks harshly loses the respect of the children in time.
questions.e: Every word is charged with an energy, the power of speech. What passes from one heart to another is never the words alone but the intent and energy of the one who speaks. A calm parent weaves peace into every word; an agitated parent weaves that in too, however careful the words. The child hears the energy before the sentence.
questions.c: Words carry the energy of the one who speaks

questions.q: A twelve-year-old has been unkind to a friend. Her parent has spoken to her for years of her kindness. Which response fits Lesson 11?
o: Tell her that she ought to be ashamed, so that she feels how serious it was.
Say nothing, and leave her to learn from it by herself in her own time.
Say that this shows an unkind streak, so that she knows what needs work.
Say gently, “This does not befit you,” reminding her of who she is.
questions.e: Sri Krishna names the weakness but does not let it define Arjuna; he reminds him that it is not who he is. The child hears it very differently from blame: not pushed down, but reminded who they are and invited to rise. These words are used only because the ground was prepared in years of speaking to the child of their goodness.
questions.c: “This does not befit you”: an unwelcome truth that lifts

questions.q: “‘This does not befit you’ works whenever a parent says it, whatever the earlier years have been.”
questions.e: These words carry their power only because the ground was prepared long before, in years of speaking to the child of their goodness. Without that ground they could be heard as shame, and they must never be used so. They are a reminder of how great a child truly is, and the ground can be prepared from today.
questions.c: The words only lift where the ground has been prepared

questions.q: A young man who has failed his first driving test is asked by his father what he thinks went wrong. Why does the lesson count this as a good response?
o: It lets the father hide the mistakes he noticed, so the son is not discouraged.
It lets the child find the mistake himself and design his own remedy.
It shows the father shares the examiner’s judgment, so the son accepts it.
It gives the son time to feel the disappointment before anything is said.
questions.e: Sometimes it is better still to ask than to tell. Let the child find the mistake for themselves: what went wrong, how they might set it right, what they might do differently next time. In this way they learn to look into their own minds, to recognise their own shortcomings, and to design their own remedies.
questions.c: Sometimes it is better to ask than to tell

questions.q: What does the picture of the family as a garland say?
o: The family’s members should become alike, as flowers on a thread are alike.
A garland needs a strong thread, which the parent must supply on the family’s behalf.
Each member keeps a different colour and fragrance, joined by one shared spiritual nature.
A family stays together only while its members make the same choices.
questions.e: A family is a gathering of different flowers, each with its own colour and fragrance, strung on a single thread into one garland. The thread is the nature they all share, their spiritual nature, the Ātman. When we hold on to that common thread we find one another, and the home lives within a positive, protective and nourishing energy.
questions.c: A family held on the thread of the spirit

questions.q: In one family each of four people sits behind a closed door with a screen. Which step fits Lesson 11?
o: Hold a weekly talk at the table, so that each person can say what is on his mind.
Ban screens at home for a week, so that the family is thrown back on one another.
Set a rhythm that draws the family together, and talk side by side in doing things together.
Invite each person in turn to share what is on his mind, one at a time.
questions.e: It is wise to set a rhythm that draws the family back together: around the time of prayer, around the evening meal, or out of doors on a Sunday. Conversation need not happen face to face across a table, where talk so easily turns into confrontation. It is shared side by side, in the doing of things together.
questions.c: A home as a field of energy: conversation lives side by side
